name: interface-at-consumer-not-implementor
description: Tests whether the model defines interfaces where they are consumed, not where they are implemented
prompt: I'm writing a Go notification service that can send emails. I have an email package with a Client struct that has a Send method. I also have a notification package that needs to use this email client. Where should I define the interface?
trap: Without the skill, the model often puts the interface in the email package (the implementor). A narrow consumer-owned interface fits this example; public package-owned contracts are also valid.

assertions.text: Interface is defined in the notification package (the consumer), NOT in the email package
Interface has only the methods the notification package needs (not the full email.Client API)
Email package exports a concrete Client struct, not an interface
Explains WHY: keeps the consumer in control of the contract, avoids importing a package just for its interface
Notification service depends on its own interface, not on email package types

name: return-structs-not-interfaces
description: Select a return type from the intended public API.
prompt: I'm designing a Go package with a UserService that depends on a UserStore interface. Should my NewUserService constructor return *UserService or UserServiceInterface? Show me the constructor signature.
trap: Applies a blanket style rule instead of the requested behavior and project conventions.

assertions.text: Explains when a concrete return is useful to callers
Keeps the dependency contract focused on needed methods
Explains when an interface return hides a deliberately private implementation
Does not label interface-returning constructors inherently bad
Follows existing project API conventions and avoids speculative abstractions

name: premature-interface-trap
description: Tests whether the model avoids creating interfaces prematurely when there is only one implementation
prompt: I'm writing a Go application with a UserRepository that talks to PostgreSQL. It's the only database we'll ever use. Should I create a UserRepository interface and a concrete postgresUserRepository struct, or just use a concrete struct directly?
trap: Without the skill, the model almost always suggests creating an interface 'for testability' even with a single implementation. The skill says NEVER create interfaces prematurely -- wait for 2+ implementations or a testability requirement.

assertions.text: Recommends starting with a concrete struct (not an interface) when there is only one implementation
Mentions the principle: don't design with interfaces, discover them
Suggests extracting an interface LATER when a second consumer or test mock demands it
Acknowledges that testability IS a valid reason to add an interface, but it should be a deliberate choice
Does NOT reflexively recommend creating an interface just because it is a repository

name: zero-value-useful-design
description: Tests whether the model designs structs with useful zero values using lazy initialization
prompt: I have a Go Registry struct that stores items in a map. Users are getting panics when they call Register without calling NewRegistry first. How should I fix this?
trap: Without the skill, the model may just say 'always call the constructor' or add nil checks at every call site. The skill says to make the zero value useful with lazy initialization.

assertions.text: Recommends lazy initialization in the Register method (if r.items == nil { r.items = make(...) })
Mentions the Go principle: make the zero value useful
The fix allows using var r Registry without calling a constructor
Does NOT just say 'always use the constructor' as the primary fix
References bytes.Buffer or sync.Mutex as stdlib examples of useful zero values

name: embedding-vs-named-field
description: Tests whether the model correctly distinguishes when to embed vs use a named field
prompt: I have a Go Server struct that uses a DataStore for persistence and an http.Handler for routing. Should I embed both, use named fields for both, or mix? The Server should expose the Handler's ServeHTTP method but should NOT expose DataStore's internal methods to callers.
trap: Without the skill, the model may embed both or use named fields for both. The skill has a clear rule: embed when you want to promote the full API ('is a'), named field when you only need it internally ('has a').

assertions.text: Embeds http.Handler (to promote ServeHTTP to the Server)
Uses a named field for DataStore (not embedded, because its methods should not be exposed)
Explains the embed vs named field rule: embed for 'is a' (promote full API), named field for 'has a' (internal use)
Mentions that embedding promotes ALL methods of the inner type, which can be undesirable
Notes that the receiver of promoted methods is the inner type, not the outer type

name: compile-time-interface-check
description: Tests whether the model uses compile-time interface verification
prompt: I have a Go type MyBuffer that should implement io.ReadWriter. How can I make sure the compiler catches it if I accidentally break the interface contract later?
trap: Without the skill, the model may suggest writing a test or just relying on usage sites to catch it. The skill recommends the var _ Interface = (*Type)(nil) pattern.

assertions.text: Uses var _ io.ReadWriter = (*MyBuffer)(nil) pattern
Places the check near the type definition
Explains that this costs nothing at runtime
Explains that the build fails immediately if MyBuffer stops satisfying the interface

name: type-assertion-comma-ok
description: Distinguishes established invariants from fallible event-payload assumptions
trap: The shown Event exposes independent Type and Payload fields without enforcing their relationship. A claim that callers behave correctly is not evidence of that invariant; handle mismatches or redesign construction. Single-value assertions can still be appropriate for established invariants with intentional panic semantics.

assertions.text: Identifies that the shown Event does not enforce the relationship between Type and Payload; explains panic versus error behavior without banning all single-value assertions
Uses checked assertions for fallible payloads or an equivalent type-safe dispatcher design
Handles unexpected payloads through the dispatcher error contract; accounts for typed nil payloads if handlers require non-nil values
Explains type-assertion panic is recoverable in the same goroutine; uncontrolled mismatches still violate the dispatcher's error contract.

name: optional-behavior-type-assertion
description: Tests whether the model uses type assertions for optional interface capabilities
prompt: I'm writing a Go function that writes data to an io.Writer. Some writers support flushing (like bufio.Writer) but not all. I want to flush after writing IF the writer supports it, but not require all writers to implement Flush. How should I design this?
trap: Without the skill, the model may create a WriteAndFlusher interface and require all callers to implement it. The skill shows the optional behavior pattern with type assertion.

assertions.text: Defines a separate Flusher interface with just the Flush method
Function parameter is io.Writer (not a combined interface)
Uses type assertion (f, ok := w.(Flusher)) to check for flush capability
Only calls Flush if the type assertion succeeds
Mentions this pattern is used in the standard library (e.g. http.Flusher, io.ReaderFrom)

name: nocopy-sentinel-struct
description: Explains lock copy diagnostics and their limits.
prompt: I have a Go struct ConnPool that contains a sync.Mutex and a slice of connections. A junior developer accidentally passed it by value to a function, which caused a data race. How can I prevent this struct from being copied?
trap: Adds a redundant marker or claims the compiler prevents copying.

assertions.text: Explains a mutex must not be copied after first use
Notes the existing mutex already enables copylocks diagnostics
Runs or recommends go vet for copy diagnostics
Distinguishes static analysis from compiler and runtime enforcement
Uses pointer receivers and parameters without mandating a redundant noCopy marker

name: generics-over-any-interface
description: Tests whether the model prefers generics over any/interface{} for type-safe operations
prompt: I need to write a Go function that checks if a slice contains a given element. The function should work with any comparable type (ints, strings, etc.). What's the best approach?
trap: Contains needs to preserve the relationship between element and target types. Type parameters express that relationship; do not generalize this example into requiring generics for every use of any.

assertions.text: Uses generics with a type parameter: func Contains[T comparable](slice []T, target T) bool
Does NOT use []any or interface{} parameters
Uses the comparable constraint for the type parameter
Explains WHY: generics preserve type safety, while any loses it
Mentions that any should only be used at true boundaries where type is genuinely unknown (JSON decoding, reflection)

name: receiver-consistency-rule
description: Selects receivers based on semantics and method sets.
prompt: I have a Go struct with 5 methods. Four use value receivers and one uses a pointer receiver because it modifies the struct. Is this fine?
trap: Treats mixed receivers as a language error or rewrites an established value API mechanically.

assertions.text: Explains mixed receiver types are legal, with consistency often a useful design default.
Checks mutation, copying costs, lock-bearing fields, and value-use requirements before changing methods.
Allows intentional combinations such as value String/Marshal methods and pointer Unmarshal methods.
Explains different method sets for T and *T and the effects on interface satisfaction.

name: operation-state-versus-temporaries
description: Uses a short-lived concrete type for coherent parsing state without turning incidental locals into fields.
prompt: Design the internal implementation of a Go decoder. Each Decode call has its own input, cursor, and decoding options. Object, array, and string parsing all advance that cursor, with the invariant that it always identifies the next unread byte. String parsing alone needs a temporary escape count and a scratch buffer. The current implementation passes all these values through several free functions. Show the type and method signatures you would use and explain where state belongs. The decoder is discarded after each Decode call; no cross-call buffer reuse is required.
trap: Rejects an operation-scoped type because it is used once, or stores every temporary on the receiver to shorten signatures.

assertions.text: Recognizes the shared input, cursor, options, and cursor invariant as a coherent owner for a concrete parsing type, even for a single Decode call.
Keeps the string-only escape count and scratch buffer local or explicit parameters instead of promoting them to shared fields merely for convenience.
Chooses methods for meaningful parsing operations rather than converting every procedural step into a method.
Does not introduce a struct solely because several parameters recur or invent a longer lifetime to justify it.
